nodes.question: What platform was used to create the online survey for HIA research?
nodes.answer: The Qualtrics platform was used to develop the short anonymous self-administered online survey.
nodes.paragraph: Development in HIA research is needed to address gaps and advance the field. Methods - approach to developing the research agenda To develop a research agenda for HIA, we followed sev - eral steps using a mixed method approach to data and evidence collection including a survey, and qualitative interactive workshops [ 30] (see Fig. 1). Data collection Phase 1: Developing ideas Phase 1 involved an international survey of HIA practi - tioners. We developed a short anonymous self-admin - istered online survey using the Qualtrics platform (see Haigh et al. BMC Public Health (2025) 25:791 supplementary document 2). Ethical approval was granted by University of New South Wales Human Ethics Advisory Panel (HC220581). An invitation to complete the survey was circulated through existing email net - works including the HIANET, the International Associa - tion for Impact Assessment HIA section, the European Public Health Association HIA Section, Society of Prac - titioners of HIA, and the International Union for Health Promotion and Education Global Working Group on HIA. The survey was open for 14 weeks between August and December 2022.

nodes.question: Where can supplementary information related to the study be found?
nodes.answer: Supplementary information can be found online at the provided DOI link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s10980-25-2065-5.
nodes.paragraph: Abstract Context Urban landscapes present a diverse matrix of structures and habitats containing significant phys- ical and behavioural barriers to terrestrial wildlife dispersal. Yet, our understanding of these barriers for large mammals in the context of genetic connectivity within urbanising landscapes is limited. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at https:// doi. org/ 10. 1007/ s10980- 25- 2065-5. C. Urbanek G. Conroy J.X. Leon K. Hohwieler Present Address: E. Brunton (*) School of Science, Technology and Engineering, University of the Sunshine Coast, 90 Sippy Downs Drive, Sippy Downs, QLD, Australia e-mail: rebrunton@usc.edu.au C. Urbanek e-mail: chris.urbanek@outlook.com G. Conroy e-mail: gconroy@usc.edu.au J. X. Leon e-mail: jleon@usc.edu.au K. Hohwieler e-mail: khohwie1@usc.edu.au G. Conroy Centre for Bioinnovation, University of the Sunshine Coast, 90 Sippy Downs Drive, Sippy Downs, QLD, Australia Landsc Ecol (2025) 40:58 58 Vol: (1234567890) on the structure of the landscape, and influenced by anthropogenic structures. As such, emphasis on gene flow pathways of M. giganteus, and other large mammals, is required in conservation planning.
